questions.question: What is the rule about driving a motor vehicle outside official roads in Iceland?
options: It is allowed for any four-wheel-drive vehicle
It is allowed everywhere outside the national parks
It is allowed within 100 metres of any road
It is prohibited, because the soil is easily damaged
questions.explanation: Tracks cut into Iceland's fragile soil and vegetation can take years or decades to heal, so off-road driving is banned and drivers caught doing it face a heavy fine.

questions.question: In which situation may a driver leave the official road without breaking the rule?
options: When the ground is dry after a long warm spell
When a thick layer of snow covers the vegetation
When the official road is closed for repair work
When another vehicle has already left tracks there
questions.explanation: The exception applies only when it is quite clear that the risk of damaging vegetation is negligible; deep winter snow cover is the example the book gives.

questions.question: Approximately how many traffic accidents happen in Iceland in an average year?
options: About 1,350
About 7,500
About 900
About 15,000
questions.explanation: Of roughly 7,500 accidents a year, around 900 involve injury, and in those about 1,350 people are hurt, so the smaller figures describe subsets, not the total.

questions.question: Which number do you dial for the emergency hot-line in Iceland?
questions.explanation: 112 reaches the single Icelandic emergency line for police, ambulance and fire service; the other numbers are foreign or non-emergency services.

questions.question: Nobody is injured in a minor collision. What must the parties involved do?
options: Fill out a traffic accident report at the scene
Exchange phone numbers and then drive away
Report to the police within twenty-four hours
Photograph the cars and send the pictures later
questions.explanation: The report must be completed on the scene no matter how insignificant the incident looks, and each party keeps one of its two copies for the insurance company.

questions.question: Which circumstance means the police should be called to a collision?
options: One of the drivers is a visitor from abroad
One of the vehicles must be towed from the scene
One of the drivers has no report form in the car
One of the drivers has no valid driving licence
questions.explanation: The police must be involved when the parties disagree about the cause, when a driver is suspected of driving under the influence, or when a driver has no valid licence.

questions.question: In mixed traffic of cars, cyclists and pedestrians, which group is most exposed?
options: Car drivers and passengers
Drivers of small vehicles
Cyclists and pedestrians
Pedestrians who are crossing
questions.explanation: Cyclists and pedestrians have no bodywork, belts or airbags around them, so both groups are far more vulnerable than anyone travelling inside a car.

questions.question: Why should the hazard warning lights be switched on at the scene of an accident?
options: To show the police which car caused it
To inform and warn the other road users
To indicate the road is closed to all traffic
To make the warning triangle unnecessary
questions.explanation: The hazard signal makes the scene visible to approaching traffic; it warns others but does not replace the warning triangle, which is still needed.

questions.question: When does traffic law require a road user to help at an accident with injured people or animals?
options: Only when he was one of the parties involved
Only when the police have requested his assistance
Only when he has completed a first aid course
Whenever he can help, whether or not he was involved
questions.explanation: The duty to give whatever assistance you can applies to every road user; it falls away only when enough people are already helping and more would just be in the way.

questions.question: How is first aid defined in the book?
options: Care given to preserve life until professionals arrive
Medical treatment given by a doctor at the scene
Transport of the injured to the nearest hospital
The examination paramedics make when they arrive
questions.explanation: First aid is the help given to someone suddenly ill or injured to preserve life, stop the condition worsening and aid recovery while professional help is on its way.

questions.question: According to the Icelandic Red Cross, what is the first step at a serious accident?
options: Call the emergency hot-line straight away
Assess the injuries of everyone involved
Secure the scene against any further accidents
Give first aid to the worst injured person
questions.explanation: The order is secure the scene, assess injuries, call for help, then give first aid; securing comes first so that helpers and casualties are not hit by passing traffic.

questions.question: Whose safety must you attend to first when you reach an accident scene?
options: That of the most seriously injured person
Your own safety, before that of anyone else
That of the other drivers who were involved
That of the traffic passing by the scene
questions.explanation: A helper who is struck by an approaching vehicle becomes another casualty and helps nobody, so personal safety is checked before the safety of others.

questions.question: Where traffic is slow and road visibility is good, how far from the scene should the warning triangle stand?
options: About 20 metres
About 100 metres
About 50 metres
About 150 metres
questions.explanation: Roughly 50 metres is enough in slow traffic with clear sight lines; faster traffic or poor visibility calls for a considerably greater distance.

questions.question: What should be done about the engine of a car that has been in an accident?
options: Make sure it has stopped, or switch it off at once
Leave it idling so the hazard lights keep working
Leave it running to keep the injured people warm
Start it again to move the wreck off the road
questions.explanation: A running engine and a damaged battery are ignition sources, and leaking petrol can be set alight by the smallest spark, so the engine is stopped immediately.

questions.question: At roughly what speed does an airbag inflate?
options: About 300 km/h
About 100 km/h
About 200 km/h
About 500 km/h
questions.explanation: An airbag deploys at around 300 km/h, fast enough to seriously injure or kill a helper working close to it, which is why undeployed bags must be disabled first.

questions.question: How should undeployed airbags be made safe before you help someone inside the car?
options: Disconnect the battery and start helping at once
Disconnect the battery and wait about a minute
Switch off the ignition and take out the key
Cut the seat belts and pull out the airbag fuse
questions.explanation: The waiting minute lets any residual charge drain from the system; without it the bag can still fire even though the battery is already disconnected.

questions.question: Several people reach an accident scene at the same time. Who should take charge?
options: The one with most first aid experience and knowledge
The person who arrived at the scene first
The oldest of the people who are present
The driver who was involved in the accident
questions.explanation: One clear leader avoids duplicated and contradictory action, and the most experienced helper is best placed to divide tasks such as first aid and calling 112.

questions.question: After how long without breathing does incurable brain damage become likely?
options: One to two minutes
Ten to twelve minutes
Three to five minutes
Fifteen minutes or more
questions.explanation: Brain tissue starts dying within a few minutes without oxygen, which is why breathing is the very first thing checked on an injured person.

questions.question: An unconscious person is injured on one side only. On which side is he placed in the recovery position?
options: On his injured side
On whichever side is easier to reach
On his back with the head turned aside
On his uninjured side
questions.explanation: Lying on the sound side keeps weight off the injury; the exception is facial or lung wounds, where the person is turned onto the harmed side instead.
